title: Moneybox Cash ISA Review
meta_title: Moneybox Cash ISA Review 2026: The 4th Withdrawal Trap
meta_description: Moneybox pays 4.71% AER, but a 4th withdrawal drops you to 0.75%. And its 16-bank FSCS structure has a catch nobody mentions.
intro:
Moneybox advertises 4.71% AER (variable) on its Cash ISA, a new-customer rate dated 6 October 2026. Two details decide whether you keep it: 1.26 percentage points is a bonus that expires after 12 months, and a fourth withdrawal in any 12-month period collapses your rate to 0.75% AER for the rest of that period.

That second number is the one to sit with. It is not a small trim — it is a fall of more than three percentage points, triggered by an action most savers would consider entirely normal. Letting your balance drop below £500 does the same thing.

There is also a second, quieter product. The Open Access Cash ISA pays 3.80% AER, opens from £1, and allows unlimited withdrawals with no penalty at all. For a lot of people that is the better account, and Moneybox does not push it nearly as hard.

sections.heading: 0.75%: what the fourth withdrawal actually costs
sections.html:
On a £10,000 balance the difference between 4.71% and 0.75% is roughly £396 a year. One withdrawal too many, and that is what you forfeit for the remainder of the 12-month window.

The window rolls continuously. It does not reset in April with the tax year. A withdrawal made in March still counts against you the following February, which is far less intuitive than it sounds and is where most of the anger in savings forums comes from.

One caveat worth being straight about: Moneybox's own pages are inconsistent on whether the free allowance is three withdrawals or four. The main product page says three per year; a support article says four are free. Assume three. If you are near the limit, contact them before moving money rather than relying on either page.

The consequence is simple. This is not an emergency fund. An emergency fund exists precisely for unpredictable access, and this account charges you heavily for it. It suits money with a known destination — a deposit, a tax bill, a wedding — where three touches a year is a realistic ceiling.

sections.heading: The 16-bank FSCS panel, and the risk hidden inside it
sections.html:
This is the genuinely unusual thing about Moneybox and almost nobody explains it properly.

Moneybox does not hold your money. It is not a bank. Cash ISA deposits are spread across a panel of sixteen institutions under client-asset rules, including Nationwide, HSBC, Barclays, NatWest, Santander and Starling alongside several international banks. Moneybox states it will never hold more than 50% of the total with any single bank.

The upside: each of those banks carries its own FSCS limit of £120,000. In principle your total protection can exceed the £120,000 you would get at a single bank.

The downside, which is the part that matters to most people: if you already bank with one of those sixteen, your Moneybox money may be aggregated with your existing balance at that institution for FSCS purposes. Someone with £100,000 at Nationwide and a large Moneybox ISA could find their effective cover is lower than they assumed, not higher.

None of the four bank or building society ISAs alongside this one carry that complication. If you hold significant balances at a high-street bank already, this is worth ten minutes of checking before you deposit.

sections.heading: The bonus expiry, in money rather than percentages
sections.html:
On £10,000 the 1.26% bonus is worth about £126 across the first year. After twelve months the rate reverts to 3.45% variable — and that underlying rate has not moved since this page was first written, which is the detail that matters. Every penny of the increase from 4.00% to 4.71% is bonus, so the rate you drop to in year two is exactly what it always was.

The direction of travel says the same thing. Moneybox advertised 4.26% in March 2026, 4.00% in August and 4.71% in October, while the underlying rate sat at 3.45% throughout. The headline is a marketing dial; the floor underneath it is not moving.

Practically, this is a diarised account. Set a reminder for month eleven, compare 3.45% against the market, and transfer if it has slipped. ISA transfers preserve the wrapper, so moving costs nothing but a form. Savers who genuinely will not look again are better off with a flat-rate provider and no bonus mechanic.

sections.heading: Should you take the Open Access version instead?
sections.html:
For a large share of savers, yes.

The Open Access Cash ISA pays 3.80% rather than 4.71%. On £10,000 that gap is about £91 a year — and this is where the answer has changed. When the headline was 4.00% the gap was around £20, which was a trivial price for removing the withdrawal cliff. At £91 it is a real decision.

In exchange for that £91 you get a £1 minimum instead of £500 and unlimited penalty-free withdrawals instead of a 0.75% cliff edge. So the test is now arithmetic rather than obvious: if there is a realistic chance of a fourth withdrawal, the cliff costs £396 and the insurance costs £91, and you take the insurance. If you are confident the money will sit still for a year, take the 4.71% and diarise month eleven. Note that the Open Access rate carries its own 0.55% bonus over a 3.25% underlying rate, so it expires too.

pros: Competitive headline rate during the first 12 months
Open Access variant offers 3.80% with unlimited withdrawals from £1
Interest accrues daily and is paid on the first of each month
Interest paid monthly, so partial months still earn
Deposits spread across 16 institutions, which can raise total FSCS cover
Accepts transfers in, including from older building society ISAs
cons: A 4th withdrawal collapses the rate to 0.75% AER — roughly £325 a year on £10,000
Balance dipping below £500 triggers the same penalty
1.26% of the headline rate vanishes after 12 months, leaving the same 3.45% underlying rate it has paid all along
Not a flexible ISA, so anything you withdraw cannot be replaced without using fresh allowance
Moneybox's own pages disagree on whether 3 or 4 withdrawals are free
No branch, no joint account, no phone-based account management
verdict: The Open Access version at 3.80% still removes the withdrawal cliff, but it now costs about £91 a year on £10,000 rather than £20, so it is no longer the automatic answer it was two months ago. Take the headline 4.71% account if the money has a known purpose and will be touched three times a year or fewer, and diarise the bonus expiry at eleven months; take Open Access if a fourth withdrawal is plausible, because the cliff costs £396 and the insurance costs £91. Either way, this is not a flexible ISA — Moneybox says so in its own terms — so money you withdraw cannot be put back without using fresh allowance. And if you already hold a large balance with Nationwide, HSBC, Barclays, NatWest or Santander, check the FSCS aggregation position before depositing anything substantial.

faqs.q: What happens on the fourth withdrawal?
faqs.a: Your rate drops to 0.75% AER for the remainder of the rolling 12-month period. On £10,000 that is roughly £325 of lost interest. The window rolls continuously rather than resetting with the tax year.

faqs.q: Is the 4.71% rate guaranteed for a year?
faqs.a: No. It is variable, and it includes a 1.26% bonus that runs for 12 months. Both the underlying rate and the headline can change. Moneybox advertised 4.26% in March 2026, 4.00% in August and 4.71% in October, with the underlying rate at 3.45% throughout.

faqs.q: How much is my money protected for?
faqs.a: The FSCS limit rose to £120,000 per banking licence on 1 December 2025. Moneybox spreads deposits across 16 institutions, each with its own limit — but if you already hold money at one of those banks, the balances may be combined when cover is calculated.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the two Moneybox cash ISAs?
faqs.a: The Cash ISA pays 4.71% AER, needs £500 to open, and penalises the fourth withdrawal. The Open Access Cash ISA pays 3.80% AER, opens from £1, and allows unlimited withdrawals with no penalty. Neither is a flexible ISA.

faqs.q: Can I transfer an existing ISA in?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the provider's transfer process rather than withdrawing and re-depositing, which would consume your annual allowance.

title: Nationwide Cash ISA Review
meta_title: Nationwide Cash ISA Review 2026: Fixed Beats Easy Access
meta_description: Nationwide's fixed ISAs run to 4.70% over five years and lead this comparison. Its easy-access ISA at 3.30% does not. Know which one you want.
intro:
Nationwide is really two propositions wearing one brand, and conflating them is how savers end up in the wrong account.

Its fixed-rate ISA ladder is the best of any provider compared here — 4.50% for one year, 4.55% for two, 4.65% for three and 4.70% for five. That five-year rate is the highest fixed figure in this comparison, though Moneybox now advertises 4.71% on a variable rate with conditions attached to it.

Its easy-access offering is not competitive. The 1 Year Triple Access ISA pays 3.30% and cuts you to 1.05% on a fourth withdrawal — a worse rate and a similar penalty to app-based rivals paying 3.80% or more with fewer strings.

Decide which you actually need before looking at Nationwide, because the answer changes completely depending on the timeframe.

sections.heading: The fixed-rate ladder, and why the five-year is the interesting one
sections.html:
Most providers price the long end conservatively because they do not want to be locked into a high rate if the base rate falls. Nationwide has done the opposite: 4.70% for five years, which is 20 basis points above its own one-year rate.

With the Bank of England base rate held at 3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting in July 2026, a five-year fix above 4.5% is a bet that rates drift down from here. If that view is right, locking in now looks smart in three years' time. If rates rise instead, you are stuck — and Nationwide's early access terms mean closure and a charge, not a partial withdrawal.

The shorter terms are competitive rather than exceptional. Leeds Building Society used to edge Nationwide at one year; Nationwide has now risen to match it, and both pay 4.50% at one year and 4.55% at two. Nationwide still takes the longer terms, but only just — 4.65% against Leeds’ 4.60% at three years and 4.70% against 4.65% at five. If you are laddering across terms, pick the short end on service rather than rate, and Nationwide for three years or longer.

sections.heading: Why the Triple Access ISA is the weak link
sections.html:
The 1 Year Triple Access ISA pays 3.30% AER with three withdrawals permitted. A fourth cuts the rate to 1.05%.

Set against the alternatives, that is hard to justify. Moneybox's Open Access ISA pays 3.80% with unlimited withdrawals and no penalty at all. Its headline Cash ISA pays 4.71%, bonus included. Trading 212 pays 3.6%, from £1, tracking the Bank of England base rate less 0.15 points.

So Nationwide asks you to accept a lower rate and a withdrawal cap, which is the wrong side of both trades. Unless you specifically want your ISA sitting beside a Nationwide current account, there is no rate argument for this account.

sections.heading: The mutual angle, and how much to weight it
sections.html:
Nationwide is a building society, not a bank, and it does return money to members. From 10 June 2026 it paid £100 each to around 4.4 million members under its Fairer Share scheme — roughly £440 million in total.

One important caveat: eligibility requires a Nationwide current account plus a qualifying savings or mortgage product. Whether a cash ISA counts as a qualifying savings product is not something we could verify, and it has varied between years. If the £100 is part of your calculation, read the current year's terms before assuming an ISA qualifies. Do not open an account on the strength of it.

Nationwide also scored 77% for customer satisfaction in Which?'s August 2026 survey, joint highest here. That is a genuine strength and it is consistent across years.

sections.heading: The complaints picture, honestly
sections.html:
Nationwide's own published data for April to September 2025 records 63,947 banking and credit complaints with 52.41% upheld, at a rate of 1.94 complaints per 1,000 accounts. The most common cause was general administration and customer service.

3,001 cases reached the Financial Ombudsman in the second half of 2025, up 69% on the first half.

Two things are true at once. Nationwide scores well on customer satisfaction surveys and poorly on complaint volume trends. The likeliest reading is that the median experience is good — hence 77% — while the tail of problems is growing. If your money is going into a fixed account you will not touch for years, this matters less than it would for a current account.

pros: 5-year fixed at 4.70% AER — the highest fixed rate in this comparison
3-year fixed at 4.65% also leads the field
Which? customer score of 77%, joint highest here
Mutual structure, with £100 Fairer Share paid to ~4.4m members in June 2026
Branch network alongside app and online access
Full fixed-rate ladder from one to five years in one place
cons: Triple Access ISA at 3.30% is well behind app-based rivals paying 3.80–4.56%
A 4th withdrawal on Triple Access cuts the rate to 1.05%
Early access on fixed accounts means closing the account and paying a charge
Leeds Building Society beats the 1-year fix (4.50% against 4.40%)
3,001 FOS cases in H2 2025, up 69% on the previous half
52.41% of its own banking complaints upheld, April to September 2025
Sole accounts only, no joint option
verdict: Use Nationwide for fixed-term money and look elsewhere for anything you might need. The three and five-year fixes at 4.65% and 4.70% are the strongest rates in this comparison, and if you believe the base rate drifts down from 3.75%, the five-year is a genuinely good bet. Avoid the Triple Access ISA — it is beaten on rate and on flexibility by several rivals simultaneously. If you are laddering, there is now nothing between Nationwide and Leeds at one and two years, so choose on service; Nationwide takes anything three years or longer by five basis points.

faqs.q: Is the five-year fix at 4.70% worth locking into?
faqs.a: It depends on your rate view. With the base rate at 3.75% and held for five consecutive meetings, 4.70% for five years pays you a premium for committing. If rates fall, it looks excellent. If they rise, you cannot access the money without closing the account and paying a charge.

faqs.q: Can I withdraw early from a Nationwide fixed ISA?
faqs.a: Not partially. Early access means closing the account and paying an early access charge. Fixed accounts should only hold money you are confident you will not need.

faqs.q: Does a cash ISA qualify me for the £100 Fairer Share payment?
faqs.a: We could not verify this. Eligibility requires a Nationwide current account plus a qualifying savings or mortgage product, and which products qualify has changed between years. Check the current terms before counting on it.

faqs.q: How does Nationwide compare with Leeds Building Society?
faqs.a: They are level at one year, both at 4.50%, and level at two, both at 4.55%. Nationwide wins at three years (4.65% against 4.60%) and five (4.70% against 4.65%), but by five basis points rather than the clear margin this page previously described. Both scored 77% with Which?, though only Leeds is a Which? Recommended Provider.

faqs.q: How much of my money is protected?
faqs.a: Up to £120,000 per banking licence following the increase on 1 December 2025, or £240,000 on a joint account. Note that Nationwide and Virgin Money share a licence, so balances across both count once.

title: Leeds Building Society Cash ISA Review
meta_title: Leeds BS Cash ISA 2026: A Which? Recommended Provider
meta_description: Leeds BS is one of only eight Which? Recommended savings providers and drew 79 Ombudsman cases against a big bank's 4,596. Rates and terms in full.
intro:
Leeds Building Society is the smallest name in this comparison and the only one carrying Which? Recommended Provider status — an award given to just eight of the thirty-nine savings providers surveyed in August 2026.

The complaints gap is the number that puts it in perspective. In the second half of 2025 the Financial Ombudsman took on 79 new cases about Leeds. The figure for one large high-street bank was 4,596. Leeds is a fraction of the size, so the raw comparison is unfair — but 79 cases across an entire half-year is a very small number in absolute terms however you scale it.

It also matches the best one-year fix in this group, at 4.50% AER from a £100 minimum.

sections.heading: What Which? Recommended Provider actually means
sections.html:
The label gets used loosely, so it is worth being precise. Which? surveys customers on service and separately scores providers on the rates they pay. Recommended Provider status requires performing well on both, and it is withdrawn if either slips.

Eight providers out of thirty-nine earned it in the August 2026 survey. Leeds was one. Nationwide, with an identical 77% customer score, was not — because its interest-rate score of 70% was not high enough. Leeds scored 87% on rates.

That combination is the point. Plenty of providers buy a good rate score with a short-lived bonus and poor service. Plenty of high-street banks score adequately on service while paying badly. Doing both consistently is rarer than it should be.

sections.heading: The one-year fix is where it wins
sections.html:
At 4.50% AER, the one-year fixed ISA is the joint-strongest twelve-month rate among the providers compared here. Nationwide has risen to match it exactly; one large high-street bank pays 4.00% on equivalent terms. The minimum is £100, which is the lowest entry point of any fixed ISA in this comparison.

On a full £20,000 allowance the gap over that bank is about £100 in a single year, for an identical product with identical FSCS protection.

Beyond twelve months the picture tilts, but only just. Leeds pays 4.55% at two years, 4.60% at three and 4.65% at five; Nationwide pays 4.55%, 4.65% and 4.70%. So they are level at two years and Nationwide is ahead by five basis points at three and five — on a full £20,000 allowance that is £10 a year, which is not a reason to choose a provider. Decide the long end on service and access, not on rate.

Leeds also runs the same four terms as Monthly Income versions at identical rates, which none of the app-based rivals here offer at all. Early access costs 90 days’ interest at one year, 180 at two, 270 at three and 365 at five.

sections.heading: The complaints record is the real differentiator
sections.html:
Seventy-nine Ombudsman cases in six months, split 37 banking and 41 mortgages.

Set that beside Nationwide's 3,001 and one large high-street bank's 4,596 in the same period. Leeds is a far smaller institution and any fair comparison has to account for that — but even adjusting generously for scale, this is a provider whose customers rarely escalate.

Per-firm uphold percentages sit in an Ombudsman spreadsheet we could not access, so we cannot tell you what proportion of those 79 cases went the customer's way. The overall Ombudsman uphold rate was 32% in the first half of 2025, down from 35%, if you want a benchmark.

For a cash ISA specifically this matters less than it would for a current account or a mortgage — you deposit money and largely leave it. But it tells you something about how the organisation behaves when something does go wrong.

sections.heading: What you give up
sections.html:
Reach, mostly. The branch network is concentrated in Yorkshire and the surrounding region. If walking into a branch matters to you and you live in Cornwall, this is not a practical option.

The digital experience is also a step behind the app-first providers. Moneybox and Trading 212 are built as apps first with everything that implies for speed of opening and day-to-day management. Leeds is a traditional building society that has added online access, and it feels like it.

Two things in the variable range are worth knowing before you open one. The Online Access Cash ISA pays 4.16% but drops to 0.05% if the balance falls below £1,000, which is the sharpest cliff-edge in this comparison. And the older E-ISA and ISA Saver pay 1.45%, so an old Leeds ISA left alone is almost certainly in the wrong account. None of Leeds’ cash ISAs is a flexible ISA — money you withdraw cannot be replaced without using fresh allowance, which Trading 212 does allow.

pros: Which? Recommended Provider — one of only 8 out of 39 surveyed
Joint-best one-year fixed ISA rate here at 4.50% AER, from a £100 minimum
87% Which? interest-rate score, second highest in this comparison
Just 79 Ombudsman cases in H2 2025 — the lowest by a wide margin
Member-owned building society rather than a shareholder-owned bank
Own banking licence, so no FSCS aggregation with a larger group
cons: Branch network concentrated in Yorkshire and the surrounding area
Digital experience trails the app-first providers noticeably
Narrowly beaten by Nationwide at three and five years — 4.60% against 4.65%, and 4.65% against 4.70%
Smaller product range than the high-street banks
Rates move frequently, so published figures date quickly
verdict: The most straightforwardly recommendable provider in this comparison, and the one to choose if you want a one-year fix. It is the only Which? Recommended Provider here, it matches the best twelve-month rate at 4.50% from a £100 minimum, and its Ombudsman record is remarkable even allowing for its size. Look to Nationwide instead if you want to fix for three years or longer, and to an app-based provider if slick digital management matters more to you than service quality.

faqs.q: What makes Leeds a Which? Recommended Provider?
faqs.a: It requires performing well on both customer satisfaction and the rates paid. Leeds scored 77% on customer satisfaction and 87% on interest rates in the August 2026 survey. Only eight of thirty-nine providers qualified.

faqs.q: Is my money as safe as with a big bank?
faqs.a: Yes. FSCS protection is £120,000 per person per banking licence regardless of institution size, and Leeds holds its own licence — so balances are not aggregated with any larger group.

faqs.q: Do I need to live in Yorkshire?
faqs.a: No. Accounts can be opened and managed online or by phone from anywhere in the UK. The branch network is regional, so branch access specifically is limited outside Yorkshire and the surrounding area.

faqs.q: Should I pick Leeds or Nationwide?
faqs.a: They are level at one year and two, both paying 4.50% and 4.55%. Nationwide is five basis points ahead at three years (4.65% against 4.60%) and five (4.70% against 4.65%) — about £10 a year on a full allowance. Both scored 77% with Which?, but only Leeds holds Recommended Provider status, so on these rates service is the tie-breaker.

faqs.q: How many complaints does Leeds get?
faqs.a: Seventy-nine new Ombudsman cases in the second half of 2025 — 37 banking, 41 mortgages. One large high-street bank had 4,596 and Nationwide 3,001 in the same period, though both are much larger organisations.

title: Trading 212 Cash ISA Review
meta_title: Trading 212 Cash ISA: 3.6%, and Why It Tracks the Base Rate
meta_description: Trading 212's cash ISA pays 3.6% AER, set at the Bank of England base rate minus 0.15 points. The lowest rate here, and the only flexible one.
intro:
Trading 212's cash ISA pays 3.6% AER from £1, and the number is not set by anybody's marketing department. It is the Bank of England base rate minus 0.15 percentage points, published as a formula: with the base rate held at 3.75% since 17 September 2026, that arithmetic gives 3.60% exactly.

Two months ago this page described Trading 212 as the best rate in this comparison, at around 4.56%. It is now the lowest — below Moneybox's Open Access ISA at 3.80%, below Nationwide's fixed ladder and below Leeds. That is not a reversal of policy, it is the tracker doing exactly what it says: the rate followed the base rate down. Trading 212 still holds the highest Which? interest-rate score here at 93%, ahead of Leeds on 87% and Nationwide on 70%, but that was scored in August 2026 when the rate was a point higher, so read it as a statement about the past.

What you get instead of a market-leading rate is a rate you can predict. Every other variable account in this comparison can be repriced at the provider's discretion; this one moves only when the Bank of England moves, and Trading 212 undertakes to give 14 days' notice if it ever widens the 0.15-point margin.

The consideration is structural rather than financial. Trading 212 is an investment platform that offers a cash ISA, not a bank or building society that also does investments. That difference shapes how your money is held and what the company's attention is actually on.

sections.heading: No bonus, no minimum, no withdrawal cap
sections.html:
Every other provider in this comparison attaches a condition to its best rate. Moneybox requires £500 and penalises the fourth withdrawal at 0.75%. Nationwide's Triple Access cuts to 1.05% on a fourth withdrawal. One large high-street bank pays 0.75% unless you have £100,000. Leeds requires you to fix.

Trading 212 does none of that. One pound opens it, the rate is not propped up by an expiring bonus, and you can withdraw as often as you want without penalty. It is also the only flexible ISA in this comparison — money you take out can be put back in the same tax year without using fresh allowance. Neither Moneybox nor Leeds offers that, and Moneybox says so explicitly in its terms.

That simplicity removes the failure mode that catches most savers: the forgotten bonus expiry, the accidental fourth withdrawal, the balance that dipped below a threshold. The honest question now is what it is worth. On £10,000, Moneybox’s headline 4.71% pays about £111 more a year than 3.6%, and its Open Access account about £20 more. If you will genuinely never breach a withdrawal limit or miss a bonus expiry, those conditions cost you nothing and the extra interest is free. Trading 212 is the account for people who know they will not do the admin — and it now charges a visible premium for that.

sections.heading: An investment platform is not a bank
sections.html:
This is the part to understand properly before depositing.

Trading 212's core business is share and ETF dealing. The cash ISA is an adjacent product. That has practical consequences: cash held on investment platforms is typically placed with partner banks rather than held by the platform itself, which affects how FSCS protection applies and which institution is actually holding your money.

The Ombudsman data reflects the business mix too. Of 308 cases in the second half of 2025, 240 concerned investments and only 67 concerned banking. So most complaints are about the trading side rather than the savings side — useful context, though it also means there is less public evidence about how they handle cash ISA problems specifically.

Case volumes rose from 198 in the first half of 2025 to 308 in the second, an increase of around 56%. Per-firm uphold rates are not published on the Ombudsman's website, so we cannot tell you how those cases were decided.

sections.heading: Where the 93% rate score comes from and what it does not tell you
sections.html:
Which?'s interest-rate score reflects what a provider pays across its range relative to the market. Trading 212's 93% says it paid consistently well across the survey period, not merely that one headline product looked good on the day. It is worth being clear about the date: the survey was August 2026, when this cash ISA was paying around 4.56%. At 3.6% the same score would not be awarded today, and nobody should open the account on the strength of it.

The customer score is a different measure and sits lower at 74% — behind Leeds and Nationwide on 77%, ahead of one large high-street bank on 67%. And Trading 212 is not a Which? Recommended Provider, because that status requires strength on both measures.

Read together, the two scores say something coherent: excellent rates, decent but not exceptional service. For a cash ISA that you fund and leave, rates matter more than service. For anything where you expect to need help, the ranking would look different.

sections.heading: Who this suits and who it does not
sections.html:
It suits a rate-focused saver comfortable managing money in an app, who wants unlimited access without a penalty structure, and who does not want to diarise a bonus expiry.

It suits less well anyone who wants a traditional deposit-taker holding their money directly, anyone who may want branch or phone support, and anyone uneasy about holding cash on a platform whose main business is share dealing.

One practical point, and it is the whole case for the account: because the rate is a published tracker rather than a discretionary one, you can work out what it will be. If the Bank of England cuts to 3.50% in November, this account pays 3.35% the same day; if it holds, you stay at 3.6%. That is a different kind of certainty from a fixed rate, and a more useful one than a variable rate nobody can forecast — but it also means there is no prospect of it beating the market again unless the base rate rises.

pros: The only published rate formula here: Bank of England base rate minus 0.15 points
The only genuinely flexible ISA in this comparison — withdrawals can be replaced in the same tax year
No withdrawal limits and no penalty rate
No expiring bonus — the headline rate is the real rate
Slick app-based management and fast account opening
No minimum balance to maintain the advertised rate, and 14 days’ notice promised before the margin can widen
cons: At 3.6% it is now the lowest rate on this page, behind even Moneybox’s unrestricted Open Access ISA at 3.80%
An investment platform rather than a bank; cash sits with unnamed partner banks, with FSCS cover quoted per bank
Not a Which? Recommended Provider, and its 93% rate score was earned when the rate was around 4.56%
Customer score of 74% trails Leeds and Nationwide
Ombudsman cases rose around 56% between H1 and H2 2025
App and web only — no branch or traditional phone service
verdict: No longer the best rate here, and worth choosing for a different reason than it was two months ago. At 3.6% it pays the least of the four providers compared on this page, but it is the only one that tells you how its rate is calculated — base rate minus 0.15 points — and the only genuinely flexible ISA among them, so withdrawals can be replaced within the tax year. That combination suits a saver who wants accessible cash with no conditions to monitor and no admin to forget, and who would rather have a rate they can predict than a headline they have to re-check every few months. Anyone chasing the highest number should take Moneybox at 4.71% and diarise the bonus, or fix with Nationwide or Leeds. Check where the cash is actually held before depositing a large balance: Trading 212 says FSCS cover is £120,000 per partner bank but does not name the banks.

faqs.q: Is Trading 212 a bank?
faqs.a: No. It is an FCA-regulated investment platform whose main business is share and ETF dealing. Cash held on investment platforms is typically placed with partner banks rather than held by the platform, which affects how FSCS protection applies. Check the current arrangement before depositing a large sum.

faqs.q: Is there a catch to the rate?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. There is no bonus period, no minimum balance and no withdrawal cap. The rate is variable, but not at the provider’s discretion: it is the Bank of England base rate minus 0.15 points, so it changes when the base rate changes and Trading 212 gives 14 days’ notice if it widens that margin. The catch, such as it is, is that the formula now produces the lowest rate on this page.

faqs.q: How does it compare with Moneybox?
faqs.a: Moneybox pays more on both of its accounts now. Its headline Cash ISA is 4.71%, though that needs £500, includes a bonus that expires after 12 months and drops to 0.75% on a fourth withdrawal; its Open Access account pays 3.80% with unlimited withdrawals. Trading 212's 3.6% is below both. What Trading 212 has that neither Moneybox account has is a published rate formula and a genuinely flexible ISA.

faqs.q: How many complaints does it get?
faqs.a: 308 new Ombudsman cases in the second half of 2025, up from 198 in the first half. Most — 240 — concerned investments rather than banking.

faqs.q: Can I transfer an existing cash ISA in?
faqs.a: Yes, using the platform's transfer-in process. Never withdraw and re-deposit, as that would use up your annual ISA allowance.
